sources.news_title: Ages 5, 8, and 11: Inside the Oregon School Shooting That Killed Three Children and a Teacher in Three Minutes
Ages 5, 8, and 11: Inside the Oregon School Shooting That Killed Three Children and a Teacher in Three Minutes
sources.text:
BEND, Ore. — Three children and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon on Thursday afternoon when a 16-year-old gunman blasted through the school's secured entrance and opened fire inside. The attack ended not with a police response but with a civilian who witnessed the teenager forcing his way in, made the decision to pursue him, and fatally shot him inside the building. Five people in total were dead by 1:02 p.m. — the four victims and the shooter himself — and two others were rushed to the hospital with critical wounds, leaving a Pacific Northwest city struggling to absorb a tragedy that consumed an entire school day in under three minutes.
Three Minutes That Left Four Dead
The chain of emergency calls began at 12:59 p.m., when a motorist contacted Deschutes County dispatch to report being shot at multiple times by a stranger armed with a long gun on a nearby street. Additional callers flooded the lines within seconds, reporting that the same person had moved to 61530 Southeast Stone Creek Lane and was firing inside the school. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at the evening press conference that officers directed the campus into lockdown at 1:01 p.m. and arrived on scene one minute later, only to find the suspect already dead.
Locked Doors Were Not Enough
Silver Rail Elementary, which serves more than 400 students from kindergarten through fifth grade, had its entrance locked when the attacker arrived. He did not search for an unlocked door. Chief Krantz told reporters that the teenager fired through the school's locked entrance to breach the building — a detail confirmed by KTVZ. While Krantz did not publicly name the weapon at the press conference, a law enforcement official briefed on the investigation separately told the Associated Press that the attacker had used a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother. Police found no prior connection between the teenager and anyone at the school, and his motive had not been established by Thursday night.
A Civilian Followed Him In
The attack ended because of a community member who happened to be nearby, not a police response. According to ABC7 News, Chief Krantz confirmed at the press conference that the civilian watched the gunman shoot through the entrance and made the active decision to follow him inside. Armed with a legally carried concealed firearm, the community member confronted the teenager inside the building and shot him dead, ending the attack within the same three-minute window. The civilian's identity had not been released as of Thursday evening. The incident will intensify an already contested national debate over the role of armed civilians in responding to school shootings.
The Victims: Ages 5, 8, 11, and a Teacher
Chief Krantz confirmed at the press conference that the three children who died were 5, 8, and 11 years old, and that the fourth victim was a teacher at the school, according to KTVZ. None of the victims had been publicly identified as of Thursday evening; officials said their families had been personally notified. Two additional people — a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher — were taken by emergency crews to St. Charles Medical Center in Bend with critical injuries, and their conditions were not confirmed at press time.
Evacuation, Reunification, and Emergency Response
Law enforcement personnel from agencies across Central Oregon converged on the campus throughout the afternoon. Officers moved through the building classroom by classroom, guiding students and staff out while investigators worked to secure the crime scene. KATU News confirmed that a family reunification site was set up at Journey Church, 61303 S. Highway 97. Parents arrived throughout the afternoon in a visible state of panic and relief, many holding children in tight embraces as word of the casualty count spread through the crowd.
Political Leaders Respond
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook addressed those connected to the school community in a statement, assuring them: "we are with you and we will stay with you." Police Chief Krantz, at the same evening briefing, told reporters: "This is something we never want to happen anywhere."
Gov. Tina Kotek attended the press conference in person and told reporters that the day had left her heartbroken. "No parent should have to have this kind of day," Kotek said, and she specifically thanked the community member whose actions ended the shooting. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler, also present at the briefing, called a school a place where children are supposed to feel secure and said flatly that what happened should never occur, as Time reported. Rep. Janelle Bynum, who represents the congressional district that includes Bend, said in a statement that the children were supposed to go to school to make friends — not to mourn them. U.S. Senator Ron Wyden issued a formal statement through his Senate office calling the violence evidence of the catastrophic consequences of congressional inaction on gun safety, and demanding passage of what he described as common-sense gun legislation.
FBI Joins the Investigation
FBI Director Kash Patel announced on social media that the bureau's Portland field office had been deployed to assist Bend Police and Oregon state authorities, pledging that every available federal resource would be made available to the investigation, according to Time. Federal and local investigators spent Thursday evening reviewing surveillance footage, documenting the crime scene, and attempting to build a profile of the unnamed 16-year-old suspect. The school was expected to remain closed for several days as a crime scene while investigators completed their work.
Bend Mourns — and the Nation Counts
Hundreds of Bend residents gathered at Drake Park on Thursday evening for a candlelight vigil, standing in collective grief for children and a teacher who had not come home. Bend is a city of roughly 100,000 in central Oregon — a place associated more readily with outdoor recreation and mountain trails than with violent crime — yet it has now confronted mass shootings twice in four years. A gunman killed two people at a local Safeway in August 2022 before dying by suicide; Thursday's toll is heavier and harder to process.
The national scale of the problem is relentless. A CNN analysis of data from the Gun Violence Archive, Education Week, and Everytown for Gun Safety identified the Silver Rail attack as the 36th shooting on a K-12 campus in the United States in 2026, and the 52nd at any school this year. For three families in Bend, Oregon, those numbers carry a weight no ledger can hold. Three children went to school on a Thursday morning and did not come home.

sources.news_title: The Latest: 16-year-old kills 3 children and a teacher at Oregon elementary school
sources.text:
A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school Thursday, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a man who followed him into the building, police said Friday. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called her actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured.
In a statement read to reporters on Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to the hospital in critical condition, authorities say.
Krantz identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school.
The Latest:
The news conference has ended
During the news conference, the police chief named the suspect and said he would only utter his name that one time.
The news conference lasted a little over 30 minutes.
School resource officer was at another school during shooting
The school resource officer was not at the school at the time of the shooting, authorities said.
They said the officer oversees around six other buildings and was at a nearby school.
Chief says man who killed gunman had .40-caliber pistol
Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, Giamanco entered the school, heard shots and fired his gun after seeing a teacher fighting with the shooter, Krantz said.
Just moments earlier, he had seen the gunman shooting at a truck and heading toward the school.
Krantz said the teacher “threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” the chief said.
Chief lauds heroes
“I don’t think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage,” Krantz said.
“When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The quick thinking to observe, to then park and follow someone into the school is incredible and undoubtedly saved people.
“If it came natural as a protective father, that’s terrific,” he said.
“The teacher who’s willing to stand and fight for her children — incredible,” the chief added. “We all recognize that is true heroism. We don’t see that a lot in society.”
Chief details encounters leading up to shooting
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Krantz said.
The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured, but drove off and called for help.
A second driver, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw the gunman shooting at the truck and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside.
He saw the teen wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times, Krantz said.
Mother of suspect: ‘I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something
’
The mother of the teen identified by authorities as the Oregon school shooter says her son was a ‘good boy’ as she tearfully apologized to victims and their families.
Shauntai Nickerson, the mother of Griffin John II, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun, and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
Police say motive still unclear
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” Krantz said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun.
Teacher’s family says working at school was her ‘dream job’
The family of Meghan Lambert, in a statement read by officials, said she grew up in Bend, graduated from Boise State University and had a passion for sports, especially volleyball, and was a local coach.
They said she was funny, opinionated, “fought for the underdog” and “those with special needs”
“Meg loved those children,” the family said.
As many as 15 shots were fired from 12-gauge shotgun
The gunman fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, the police chief said.
Authorities said he was a former student.
Superintendent says staff in ‘so much pain’
“This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us profoundly for years to come,” said Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook.
Teacher threw cellphone at suspect try to stop him
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz says a teacher threw a cellphone and tackled and fought with the teenage gunman to try to stop him.
The teacher’s actions likely helped save lives, the chief said, calling her actions “heroic.”
JUST IN: The 16-year-old shooter who killed 4 at an Oregon elementary school is Griffin John II, a former student, police say
JUST IN: A teacher threw a cell phone and tackled the teenage gunman who killed 4 people inside a school Thursday, police say
Mom of 6-year-old says son hid under table until gunfire stopped
Linda Sanchez’s 6-year-old son was getting escorted to the bathroom by a teacher when the two heard gunfire. They hid under a table in a nearby office until the gunfire stopped.
Soon after, Sanchez got a robocall notifying her about the lockdown at her son’s school, and then heard ambulances and police cars heading to the school where her son attends the first grade.
“My heart was just like pounding because he was in there,” Sanchez said.
Sanchez’s son was in a special education class at the time where some students went for individualized attention. Sanchez was told by school staff that the classroom was closest to the door where the gunman entered the school.
Youngest child killed in the shooting loved ‘misunderstood’ creatures, aunt says
Five-year-old Rhoam Summer liked for all of his sea creature stuffed animals to be in his favorite color: rainbow, his aunt said.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said Swan Sheridan, whose sister is Rhoam’s mother.
“He had a great fondness for sharks and dinosaurs and creatures that were in his words, ‘misunderstood,’” she said.
He was also a fast runner and a fearless climber, his aunt said.
Sheridan said her nephew would climb and jump off anything and was an “incredibly fast” runner, even from a young age. “He was a little ball of energy from the moment he was born,” she said.
“He was a very, very happy child,” she said.
A wounded teacher is recovering from surgery
A wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she underwent surgery and had injuries to her left arm and right hand.
Police responded within minutes
Some 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their childrens’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
Man who stopped the shooter has 2 daughters at the school
The man who shot the school shooter in Bend, Oregon has been identified by his mother.
Kenda Freeman said Kaylub Giamanco is a lifelong Bend resident and a father with two young daughters at Silver Rail Elementary School.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” she said, reading from a prepared statement to reporters outside her son’s residence near the school.
Freeman said the family is asking for privacy “during this difficult time” and is not giving interviews.
Trump praises ‘great hero’ who helped after Oregon school shooting
President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House he had been briefed on the shooting and praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said, saying the tragedy otherwise likely would have been much worse.
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
—- By Haven Daley, Alanna Durkin Richer and Eric Tucker
A parent says she was amazed a member of the public pursued the shooter
Brooke Olsen’s daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
Officials will provide an update on the shooting
Officials plan to hold a news conference at 2 p.m. PDT Friday at the Bend Municipal Court about the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary. They say they will provide the latest information and share resources that are available for community members.

By HAVEN DALEY and SAFIYAH RIDDLE
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school, and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
John fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun.
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
The youngest victim, just 5 years old, was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming Giamanco — said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
The attacker’s mom bought the gun he used
The shooter was found dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Krantz said. He shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said Thursday.
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer, Eric Tucker and Ben Finley in Washington; Jamie Stengle in Dallas; Gene Johnson in Seattle; Ed White in Detroit; Philip Marcelo in New York; and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

Four dead in Bend shooting: A 16-year-old boy allegedly entered Bend, Oregon’s Silver Rail Elementary School with a long gun, opened fire, and killed three children ages 5, 8, and 11, and a teacher. Another child and another teacher were injured. A bystander saw the boy “blasting his way into the school,” followed him inside, and shot and killed him.
Shout out to our corrupt oligarchs! Amazon, Microsoft, and T-Mobile donated a collective $20 million to fund President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project. This should be all the fuel Rep. Shaun Scott needs to revive his dream of a statewide big business payroll tax.
Another one for the guillotine: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges Expedia drove up hotel prices by “artificially inflating hotel rates by prohibiting hotels from offering lower rates elsewhere,” the Seattle Times reports. According to the lawsuit, hotels pay a fat commission to Expedia, which they recoup by raising prices. If a hotel doesn’t follow the rules, Expedia will punish it by moving it lower in search results.
It’s so 2001 again: A letter filled with an unknown white powder was sent to the Washington secretary of state’s election division. Law enforcement intercepted it before it got to its intended destination. But c’mon, please do not mail anthrax to the election workers. Or anyone, for that matter!
No contract for Washington Appellate Project: WAP, the state’s only non-profit appellate public defense law firm—one which handles 40 percent of Washington’s public defense appeals—hasn’t reached a deal for a new contract with the Washington State Office of Public Defense (OPD) and may have to close its doors by the end of the year, the Urbanist reports. New caseload standards set statewide and worked into the proposed OPD contract will limit how much time an attorney can spend on one case, further stressing an already stressed and under-resourced WAP. The contract dispute caused WAP to file a lawsuit against OPD.
Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, Washington Post photographer in West Bank: A mass coordinated attack occurred in the West Bank when dozens of black-clad, masked Israeli settlers descended upon Palestinian villagers as they were harvesting olives. They set groves ablaze and slung rocks. They also attacked veteran WaPo photographer Heidi Lavine in her clearly marked “PRESS” vest, knocking her to the ground, taking her phone and camera, and kicking her repeatedly. Village youths helped push the attackers back, and another journalist was able to run to help Lavine. He said the settlers had beaten her “nearly to death.”

Zacharia sat on the board up until this year.

A flying car? Elon Musk unveiled what he’s calling the world’s first flying car. Flying? Buddy, that looks more like falling with style.

sources.news_title: Good Morning, News: Children Killed in Bend Mass Shooting, Police Shoot Assault Suspect in Portland, US DOJ Sues City Over Mask Ban For Cops
sources.text:
If you appreciate the Mercury‘s interesting and useful news & culture reporting, consider making a small monthly contribution to support our editorial team. Your donation is tax-deductible. You can also subscribe and have our papers delivered!
Good morning, Portland! It may be officially fall, as the leaves have started to drop from the trees and temperatures are again reaching the high 70s. Not your typical fall weather, but by all means you can sense a change in the air. It’s back in the 60s starting Saturday.
Let’s get to the news today, most of which is devastating, infuriating, and may cause lumps to materialize in all the corporeal places where you grieve.
IN LOCAL NEWS:
Three children—ages 5, 8, and 11—and a teacher are confirmed dead after a 16-year-old child with a gun opened fire inside an elementary school in Bend, Oregon yesterday afternoon. Two other people were critically injured and hospitalized. The gunman is also confirmed dead. According to OPB, an armed community member followed the gunman as he entered Silver Rail Elementary shortly before 1 pm on Thursday, then fatally shot the shooter. The brutal incident leaves Bend, a community of roughly 100,000, reeling, confused, and grieving after another irrational incident that any respectable society would work to ensure never happens again. But this is America. This is the type of incident that conservative-liberal crossover hero Charlie Kirk—who died by gunfire just over one year ago—described as “worth it” just one week after three children and three adults were killed in a Nashville shooting in 2023.
“I think it’s worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights,” Kirk said. “That is a prudent deal. It is rational.”
On the other hand, this Mercury writer’s family member—who has worked at the elementary school and the hospital where the injured were taken—said keep an eye on the helpers in the community, and extend some grace: “Don’t forget the helpers. Not because they’re ‘heroes’ but because they’re humans.”
And in more gun violence news, the Portland Police Bureau (PPB) yesterday responded to reports of an assault in downtown Portland outside the Hotel Lucia on Southwest Broadway Street. PPB officers shot the suspect when they arrived, and he later died at a hospital. The suspect was reportedly threatening passersby, and used a box cutter to assault two people. Two adult males were injured and transported to the hospital by ambulance to be treated for their injuries, according to a PPB press release. The incident caused a chaotic scene on a busy downtown street. This is the second police shooting in Portland in three weeks. This is America.
Portland city government is back in the New York Times. A story published Thursday highlights the fight over City Councilor Mitch Green’s “spicy” tweets criticizing Portland police in 2020, which Green has shocked voters and his colleagues by not equivocating as many politicians do when faced with inconvenient media narratives. Green is up for reelection in District 4, and the story shows an interesting split between the city’s elected officials’ ideologies.
Do This, Do That is out now with some good recommendations for your weekend. This week: pumpkin paddling, miniatures, and a haunted pond.
And Mercury Music Picks has your back for some cool music events this weekend. If you get the chance, take a load off and soak in some tunes.
IN NATIONAL/WORLD NEWS:
The United States Department of Justice on Thursday sued the city of Portland over its new laws banning law enforcement from wearing masks—an expected move to keep the federal government’s secret police force, well, secret. The litigation was expected when the City Council passed the mask ban in late May, and the city attorney and Mayor Keith Wilson cautioned against passing it. Councilor Sameer Kanal, who introduced the ordinance and repeatedly tweaked its language to accommodate risk averse officials (and Portland’s police union) in the time of rising fascism, said in a statement to the Oregonian that police should be identifiable.
“While we cannot comment on the litigation,” Kanal said, “we strongly believe that law enforcement officers who are easily identifiable promote transparency in their duties and strengthen trust between agencies and the communities they serve.”
Courts have overturned local mask bans in other states and cities, including California, Virginia, New York, and Philadelphia. Oregon passed a similar ban earlier this year, but is not yet included in the US DOJ’s lawsuit. Read the full story in the Oregonian.
The federal government has issued more than a dozen subpoenas in what it calls an investigation into Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar, according to an anonymous source who spoke to the Guardian. The investigation comes just weeks before the November 3 election, in which Omar is seeking reelection. Omar, a Somalian immigrant and naturalized US citizen, has been an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and his administration, which some have suggested just might be the impetus for the investigation. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested his office is investigating potential crimes related to immigration paperwork, the Guardian reported. Federal agents raided her home earlier this week, something House Democrats have called a “rogue abuse of power.” At press time, Americans concerned with the rise of fascism and the disappearance of immigrants and refugees were still awaiting Democrats’ strongly worded letter to the president.
Sean “Diddy” Combs, the rapper, convicted conspirator, and sex trafficker, is being moved from the prison where he’s reportedly been living the high life to a new, low-security prison in Pennsylvania. By “living the high life,” we mean he was repeatedly written up by prison staff for phone violations and getting into fights. But also, NBC reported that he has been living like a VIP, using a cell phone with nude photos, drinking alcohol, getting massages, and fancy meals. More celeb prison drama at the trusty outlet, TMZ.
Ok, have a good weekend. Take a deep breath.

sources.news_title: Three Children And Teacher Killed In Oregon School Shooting
sources.text:
A shooting at a primary school in Bend, Oregon, has left three children and a teacher dead.
A 16-year-old attacker forced his way inside before being shot dead by a bystander, police say.
The suspect, whose identity has not been released, reportedly fired at locked doors to enter Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday afternoon.
Police received the first emergency call at 12:59 local time, followed by reports that the gunman had entered the school.
The children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were hospitalised in critical condition.
Authorities have not established whether the teenager had any connection to the school.
Police Chief Mike Krantz said a community member pursued the attacker inside and “engaged him”, killing him before officers arrived.
Police reached the scene three minutes later and began searching the building.
Community Grieves, Safety Concerns Grow
The tragedy has devastated the local community. School district official Steven Cook said officials were “stunned and heartbroken”.
He added that no words could adequately express the community’s grief.
Classes were cancelled on Friday to give students, families and staff time to grieve.
The shooting also renews concerns about school safety in the United States.
According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, 235 shooting incidents occurred at American schools last year, with at least 140 recorded so far this year.
As families mourn, difficult questions remain about what drove the teenager to attack.
How schools can better protect children from such violence.

Oregon school shooting renews calls for Congress to expand gun rights for police officers
sources.text:

Bill awaiting action by Senate Judiciary Committee, which includes Vermont Sen. Peter Welch
The killing of three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school Thursday, October 15, is renewing attention to federal legislation that would allow qualified active and retired law enforcement officers to carry concealed firearms in school zones and other locations where guns are generally prohibited.
The LEOSA Reform Act of 2025, H.R. 2243, passed the U.S. House last year but has remained in the Senate Judiciary Committee since May 15, 2025. Vermont Democratic Sen. Peter Welch serves on the committee.
The renewed debate follows a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old boy armed with a long gun killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher. A 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were hospitalized in critical condition.
The teenage suspect, whose name had not been released, was shot and killed by an armed community member who saw him enter the school, followed him inside and confronted him, according to Bend police.
The Bend school district does have School Resource Officers embedded in their schools. It is unclear whether one was present during the shooting.
Police said the suspect gained entry by shooting through locked doors. The first emergency call came at 12:59 PM, and officers arrived at 1:02 PM. By then, the suspect had been shot.
The incident has drawn attention to the potential role of armed citizens in stopping school shootings, although authorities have not established that the person who killed the Oregon suspect was an active or retired law enforcement officer.
Sponsored by Rep. Don Bacon, R-Nebraska, the legislation would expand the existing Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act, which allows qualified active and retired law enforcement officers to carry concealed firearms across state lines.
Under the proposed changes, those officers could carry concealed firearms and ammunition, including magazines, in school zones, national parks, certain federal facilities open to the public, and state, local and private property open to the public. The bill would also allow states to reduce the frequency of firearms qualification requirements for retired officers.
The House approved the legislation May 14, 2025, by a vote of 229-193. All 215 Republicans voting supported the measure, along with 14 Democrats. Vermont Democratic Rep. Becca Balint voted against it.
Supporters argue that expanding concealed-carry rights for trained law enforcement professionals could provide additional protection during emergencies, particularly when police officers are not immediately available.
Opponents have raised concerns about expanding firearms access in sensitive locations, including schools, and the risks of introducing additional armed individuals into emergency situations.
The legislation has not received a Senate floor vote. Its most recent recorded action was referral to the Judiciary Committee on May 15, 2025.
Welch is one of the committee’s Democratic members. Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa chairs the committee, which would have to consider the measure before it could advance through the usual legislative process.

sources.news_title: Democrats call for stricter gun laws after Oregon school shooting
sources.text:
Democrats call for stricter gun laws after Oregon school shooting
A 16-year-old shooter used a shotgun purchased by his mother to attack Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on October 15, 2026.
The shooter killed three children, ages 5, 8, and 11, and one teacher. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were critically injured.
An armed community member shot and killed the attacker after he entered the locked school building, stopping further casualties. The incident began when the shooter fired at a vehicle outside the school, generating the first emergency call at 12:59 p.m.
Police arrived within three minutes of that initial call. Officers and dispatchers then received dozens of additional reports that the shooter had entered the building.
It remains unclear whether the shooter knew anyone at the school or had attended it in earlier years. Silver Rail Elementary serves 467 students from kindergarten through fifth grade and is located about 125 miles southeast of Portland.
After the shooting, students were bused to a nearby church for family reunification. Parents embraced their children and left with comfort items including stuffed animals. The Bend-La Pine school district canceled all classes, sports, and extracurricular activities at its 32 schools the following day.
Democratic lawmakers renewed calls for gun control measures in the aftermath. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon said, “The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass common-sense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools.”
Rep. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon stated, “The epidemic of gun violence in schools across America must come to an end.” She added, “No parent should have to wonder if their child will come home at the end of the day. Children deserve to feel safe — and be safe — in school.”
Rep. Janelle Bynum of Oregon, speaking at a vigil, asked, “When are we going to step up and say enough of killing our babies? When are we going to say that we need safe schools, that we need to make sure that people who should not have firearms don’t have them? When are we going to stop making excuses? When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?”
Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico said, “Much more must be done. Not a single child should be lost to gun violence. Ever.” He referenced prior reforms after the Uvalde shooting, including enhanced background checks for buyers under 21, as insufficient.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts stated, “No family should ever have to suffer like this—and there have been over 50 school shootings just this year. Congress must do much more to prevent gun violence.” She has supported federal red-flag laws and universal background checks.
Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Gov. Tina Kotek of Oregon condemned the violence but did not call for new regulations in their statements. Several Democratic members outside Oregon echoed support for additional restrictions.
The shotgun’s ownership by the shooter’s mother has been confirmed, though authorities have not released further details on how the weapon was accessed or on the shooter’s motives. The school remains closed while investigators continue their work and families process the loss.
The bystander’s intervention has been widely noted as the factor that limited the number of casualties. Officials have not identified the community member publicly at this stage.
Vigils and canceled activities across the district have focused community attention on both the immediate aftermath and longer-term policy debates. No additional shootings or related incidents have been reported in the Bend area in the hours following the attack.

sources.news_title: Oregon bishops offer prayers following Silver Rail school shooting
sources.text: Oregon bishops offer prayers following Silver Rail school shooting October 16, 2026 By OSV News OSV News Filed Under: Feature, Gun Violence, News, World News (OSV News) — Oregon’s Catholic bishops expressed sympathy and encouraged the community to support those affected by a shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school that left five dead and two wounded. A 16-year-old opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School the afternoon of Oct. 15, killing three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher, before he was shot and killed by a person at the scene who had seen him enter the school. A 7-year-old and another teacher were also taken to a hospital with critical injuries, said Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz in a media briefing that evening. “We expect that our schools are safe places for our children and all who pass through their doors. When a tragedy like this occurs, it shakes us to our core,” wrote Bishop Thomas J. Hennen of the Diocese of Baker, whose diocesan boundaries include the city of Bend, in an Oct. 15 letter expressing his “heartfelt prayers for those whose lives were taken in the shooting.” “No family should ever have to experience such fear and heartbreak. Please know that you are not alone,” said Archbishop Alexander K. Sample of the Archdiocese of Portland in an Oct. 15 statement. “I hold you close in prayer, and the Church stands with you in this time of sorrow.” Investigation into details of the shooting is ongoing. “We are working hard to ensure that we conduct a thorough investigation,” Krantz said at the press conference. He was unable to say at this point in the investigation if the shooter had attended or had a connection to the school, what guns were used by the shooter or his pursuer, or how many shots were fired; however, the police’s initial investigation revealed the shooter forced his way into the school by shooting at locked doors. Krantz also said the families of the victims have all been notified, and that students and staff at the scene were transported by bus to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. “In the coming days, there will be opportunities to gather, including a community vigil tonight, to mourn together, honor those affected and those lost, and begin the difficult process of healing,” said Bend Mayor Melanie Keibler. Bend-Lapine School Superintendent Steve Cook said the school district is rallying crisis counselors across the region to help support the community, with counselors available at the central library starting the morning of Oct. 16. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek said the state’s Department of Emergency Management is also coordinating state support for the community. “We must come together and support each other, neighbor to neighbor, Oregonian to Oregonian,” she said. An afternoon media conference is also planned for Oct. 16, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said at the evening briefing. “It is only natural that we would be flooded with emotions at a time like this — shock, grief, fear, confusion, anger,” Bishop Hennen said. “Even as more is known about what happened, there are no adequate answers for why this happened. We can only mourn, support each other, and pledge ourselves to doing everything in our power to prevent such tragedies in the future,” he added. sources.news_title: 3 Children, 1 Adult Killed in Elementary School Shooting - Charisma Magazine Online
sources.text:
A deadly school shooting in Oregon may have been stopped by a bystander, according to police.
Three children and one adult were killed at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, according to CNN.
Police arrived at the school at about 1 p.m. to find the shooter dead.
The individual who killed the shooter “may have been a bystander,” Sheila Miller, a representative of the Bend Police Department, said.
A report from CBS News said that according to its sources, the shooter was a teenager.
A so-called “good Samaritan” then intervened to kill the shooter, CBS reported.
To order Jonathan Cahn’s new book, The Altar of Pergamon, visit Amazon.com.
At least two people were hospitalized due to the incident, police said, according to CNN.
An initial 911 call reported that an “unknown man had shot into a car” at Silver Rail Elementary School, police said.
“Within about a minute, we were receiving multiple 911 calls from within the school,” Miller said, according to ABC News.
“We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy,” Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said, according to CNN.
“We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence. No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing,” he said.
Leah Schwartz, who lives near the school, said she heard shots while walking with her husband and their dog, according to NBC News.
She said they heard three shots followed by three more shots.
“They were spaced out, which made us question whether it was gunshots or someone doing construction,” Schwartz said.
This article originally appeared on The Western Journal and is reposted with permission.

sources.news_title: Governor Kotek orders flags lowered after Bend school shooting
sources.text:
Governor Tina Kotek has ordered flags at Oregon public institutions to be flown at half-staff on Friday, Oct. 16 from sunrise to sunset, pursuant to the United States Flag Code, in remembrance of those who lost their lives on Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend.
Three children and one adult were killed. One adult and one child were injured. The sixteen-year-old shooter was shot and killed by a bystander, according to police reports.
“I want to start by thanking and praising the quick thinking and courage of the Silver Rail Elementary School staff and parents — and the first responders who rushed to the scene,” Governor Kotek said. “And to the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life, your actions carry a heavy emotional burden – and my thoughts are with you. My heart is absolutely broken. Our hearts will stay broken in the days and weeks ahead. My daily prayers will be with this community, with the children, with the parents”.
“There will be time for answering all the questions we have and search for more ways to prevent this kind of violence from happening. But for now, let us hold each other close in our grief, and put as much love into the world as possible,” Governor Kotek concluded.
Kyle Bailey is the news director for News Radio 93-9 FM and 1240 KQEN.

sources.news_title: Good guy with gun stops Oregon school massacre – The Horn News
sources.text:
A gunman massacred three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school Thursday.
But the slaughter could have been much worse without a nearby dad. By the time police got there three minutes later, the gunman was already dead, stopped by an armed citizen who chased him inside.
The 16-year-old shooter forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend just after 1 p.m. by shooting out the locks on the doors, police said.
Three students, ages 5, 8 and 11, were killed, along with a teacher. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were rushed to the hospital in critical condition.
The toll could have been far worse if not for a good guy with a gun.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the gunman was shot and killed by “a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him.”
“It looks like the shooter has been neutralized, possibly shot by a father at the school,” the dispatch audio said. Police said they would likely share more information Friday.
UPDATE: New footage shows the bystander who killed the Silver Rail Elementary School shooter in Bend, Oregon describing how close he came to being shot himself.
Five dead in Wednesday's attack, including 3 children, a teacher, and the shooter.
— CNN, Washington Post https://t.co/C6q7WOSvyf pic.twitter.com/5UGwu275CW
— EzeNews (@EzeBets) October 16, 2026
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, praised the man.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life, your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you,” Kotek said.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook fought back tears at a news conference Thursday night.
“This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places and pray that it never happens here. And it has happened here today,” Cook said.
Silver Rail has more than 400 students. All Bend-La Pine schools are closed Friday.

sources.news_title: Bystander intervenes after teen opens fire at Oregon elementary school
Who is the hero of the Oregon shooting? He prevented a massacre at Silver Rail High School in Bend
sources.text:

- US News. Five killed, two seriously injured in Oregon shooting; unidentified 16-year-old suspected shooter killed by witness
A community member who rushed toward danger during a mass shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, is being praised for helping prevent further loss of life.
The unidentified bystander confronted and fatally shot the 16-year-old suspect on Thursday, October 15, before responding police officers entered the building.
Authorities have not publicly revealed the intervening person's identity, but emergency dispatch audio reportedly suggested that the individual was a father of a student at the school.
His actions came during a devastating attack that killed three children, aged five, eight and 11, and a teacher. Another seven-year-old child and a second teacher were critically injured and taken to hospital, according to reports from the Associated Press and Oregon Public Broadcasting.
The first emergency calls came shortly before 1 p.m. local time. Initial reports described a person firing at a vehicle outside the school, before further callers alerted dispatchers that an armed suspect had entered the building.
As officers were on their way, dispatch audio shared on Broadcastify indicated that someone at the scene had intervened.
“Looks like the shooter has been neutralized – possibly shot by a father at the school,” emergency dispatchers said.
“Not sure about patients at this time. The police are arriving,” the dispatcher added.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz later confirmed that a community member had pursued the suspect after seeing him enter the school and confronted him inside. Officers arrived shortly afterward and found the teenage gunman dead.
The identity of the bystander, the weapon used and whether the individual held a concealed-carry permit have not been publicly confirmed. Officials have also not established a motive for the attack.
Oregon officials praise the bystander's courage
The intervention has drawn praise from state leaders and members of the local community, even as the scale of the tragedy has left Bend in mourning.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the emotional consequences for the person who stepped in, emphasizing that intervening in such a frightening situation can carry a lasting personal burden.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life, your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you,” Kotek said.
Kotek also expressed grief for the children, their families, school employees and others affected by the shooting. In her official statement, she urged Oregonians to support one another as the community begins to process what happened.
Kathy Sheil Smith, a fifth-grade teacher who witnessed the shooting inside the building, also praised the bystander's decision to act.
“That person saw something,” she told KPTV. “They did something, and that took its own courage. I’m just grateful that that person was able to apprehend the suspect.”
Her comments offered a glimpse into the fear experienced by staff members who were responsible for protecting children while trying to keep themselves safe. Sheil Smith said she moved her pupils into a corner of the classroom as the incident unfolded.
“I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought today is the day that I am going to die,” she said. “Save my kids.”
Oregon State Representative Vikki Breese-Iverson also expressed gratitude to emergency personnel who responded to the violence, describing the attack as senseless.
What happened at Silver Rail Elementary?
Investigators are working to establish the full sequence of events leading up to the shooting. According to reports, the suspect fired at a Toyota Tacoma in the school parking lot before forcing his way into the building.
The first police call was logged at 12:59 p.m., and officers were at the scene by approximately 1:02 p.m., according to the Bend Police Department.
The school, which serves hundreds of children, was evacuated and secured as police searched classrooms and worked to reunite students with their families. Other nearby schools also took precautionary measures while the emergency response was underway.
The attack has left families grieving and teachers confronting the trauma of a day that should have been ordinary. While the bystander's intervention ended the immediate threat, it could not undo the loss of the four victims.
Authorities have not yet released the names of those killed, and the investigation remains ongoing. For now, the person who intervened remains unidentified, with officials focusing on supporting survivors, establishing what happened and understanding how the attack unfolded.
The community's gratitude toward the bystander reflects the belief that the intervention may have prevented further casualties. But the tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary remains a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of gun violence in schools.

sources.news_title: Grief and Healing Follow Deadly Attack at Oregon Elementary School
sources.text:
Photo: Joe Kline ~ AP
BEND, Ore. ~ One day after a mass shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, families across the community are grieving the loss of three children and a teacher who were killed in the attack Oct. 15. Investigators said a 16-year-old suspect entered the school and opened fire before being confronted and fatally shot by a community member who followed him into the building.
As police continue searching for a motive, parents, students and staff are leaning on one another as they cope with the shock of the tragedy. Two victims, a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher, remain hospitalized in critical condition as the community begins the long process of healing.

sources.news_title: 3 Children, Teacher Killed in Bend School Shooting
sources.text:
A 16-year-old armed with a long gun shot his way through the locked front doors of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, early Thursday afternoon and killed three children and a teacher before an armed member of the public who had followed him into the building shot him dead, police said. Two more people, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher, were in critical condition Thursday night at St. Charles Medical Center in Bend.
The children who died were 5, 8 and 11 years old, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at an evening briefing. Their names, and the name of the teacher killed, were withheld while families were notified. The attacker was identified only as a 16-year-old Bend resident. Krantz would not say what kind of weapon he carried, how many rounds he fired or how far he got inside the school, citing an investigation that was only hours old and now involves the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives alongside Bend police and the Deschutes County Sheriff's Office.
The first call to Deschutes County dispatch came at 12:59 p.m. local time from a driver who said he was being shot at repeatedly by a person with a long gun. Within a minute, dispatch had pushed an alert to every law enforcement agency in the area, and dozens more 911 calls were coming in from inside the school, a kindergarten-through-fifth-grade building on Southeast Stone Creek Lane that serves more than 400 students with a staff of about 40. Police ordered a lockdown at 1:01 p.m. The first officers reached the school at 1:02 p.m., three minutes after the first call.
By then it was over. Krantz said an officer arriving at the scene reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen him enter the school, pursued him inside and engaged him. Officers confirmed the teenager was dead, swept the building and found the four victims, then began evacuating students and staff by bus to a reunification site at Journey Church, where parents waited in a parking lot ringed by emergency vehicles and traffic cones.
Officials declined to identify the person who stopped the attack or to say whether he had any connection to the school, how he came to be armed or how he happened to be nearby when the shooting started. Gov. Tina Kotek, who joined Krantz at the briefing and later spoke at a candlelight vigil, addressed him directly without naming him. "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you, as well," she said.
Kotek said her heart was "absolutely broken." "No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," she said. She added that the Oregon Department of Emergency Management was coordinating a response across state agencies and that the state "stands ready to support" the city. The governor said she had visited Silver Rail almost exactly a year earlier, sitting with teachers and calling parents to congratulate them on their children's attendance, and remembered the school as "beautiful."
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook called the shooting "an unthinkable tragedy" and announced that every school in the district, along with all activities and athletic events, would be closed Friday. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said a school "should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure," adding, "What happened today should never happen."
Roughly 500 people gathered that night at Drake Park, on the Deschutes River in the center of the city, holding candles while quiet music played from speakers and messages were chalked on the ground. "There is power and love in this park tonight," Kotek told the crowd. "There are simply no words for the loss we've suffered today," Kebler said.
Rep. Janelle Bynum, the Democrat whose congressional district includes Bend, flew back from Washington when she learned of the shooting. "The most heartbreaking thing, as the details have surfaced, is that we have a child involved in the killing of other children," she said in a televised interview that night. "Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities. And our kids are getting shredded and it seems as if the adults don't care." In a separate statement she said children "are supposed to do arts and crafts at school," not shelter from gunfire.
Bend is a city of roughly 100,000 people on the dry side of the Cascade Range, a former timber town that has become one of the fastest-growing places in the Pacific Northwest on the strength of its outdoor recreation, breweries and remote-work migrants from Portland, Seattle and California. Its last brush with a mass shooting came in August 2022, when a 20-year-old resident opened fire with a rifle at a Safeway grocery store on the city's east side, killing a shopper and an employee before taking his own life as police closed in. Krantz was chief then, too. That attack became part of the backdrop to Oregon's Measure 114, a voter initiative approved narrowly that November that created a permit-to-purchase system and restricted large-capacity magazines, and which has spent the years since tied up in state and federal court challenges.
Thursday's attack raises a different set of questions, and Krantz was careful not to answer any of them prematurely. The suspect was too young to buy a firearm legally from any dealer, and Oregon law since 2021 has required gun owners to store weapons locked and unloaded when they are not in the owner's control, with civil liability attaching if a minor gains access to an unsecured gun. How a 16-year-old obtained a long gun, whether it belonged to a family member, and whether anyone saw warning signs are now central to the investigation. So is the question of whether he had any connection to Silver Rail, which teaches children between the ages of roughly 5 and 11, or chose it for other reasons. Police said they had notified the suspect's family but gave no indication of motive.
The school's physical defenses appear to have worked as designed up to a point. The doors were locked, as they are at most Oregon elementary schools during the instructional day, and the lockdown order went out within two minutes of the first shot. But a locked door is a delay, not a barrier, against someone willing to fire through it, and the gap between the first shot and the first officer, however short, was long enough for four people to be killed and two more gravely wounded. The pattern mirrors other recent attacks on American schools in which the shooting was over before police arrived, and it will renew debate over whether the answer lies in hardened entrances, armed staff, earlier intervention with troubled teenagers, tighter firearm storage rules or some combination.
The role of the armed bystander is likely to be the most contested element of the story. Advocates of expanded gun carrying have long argued that armed citizens are the surest check on a shooter in the minutes before police respond, and Thursday's events in Bend will be cited as a case in point: by the police chief's own account, a civilian who happened to be present ended the attack before the first patrol car arrived. Gun-control groups counter that such interventions are rare, that they carry serious risks of misidentification when officers arrive to find more than one person with a weapon, and that the more important fact is that a teenager had a firearm in the first place. Kotek, who has backed stricter gun laws throughout her career, chose to praise the intervention and leave the policy argument for another day.
For Bend-La Pine, the district's second-largest school system east of the Cascades, the immediate work is practical and grim. Counselors were being arranged for students, families and staff, and the district said it would communicate directly with Silver Rail families about when and how the school might reopen. The 7-year-old and the 54-year-old teacher remained in critical condition late Thursday, and their condition will shape whether the official death toll of four, plus the shooter, holds.
The shooting lands in the final weeks of a midterm campaign in which Oregon's 5th Congressional District, which Bynum flipped from Republican hands in 2024, is again one of the most closely watched House races in the country, and in which gun policy has been largely crowded off the national agenda by the war with Iran, fuel prices and immigration enforcement. Whether Bend changes that is an open question. The sequence of recent mass shootings, from a Pennsylvania home where nine people including two children died earlier this month to the string of attacks on schools over the past several years, has tended to produce a brief surge of attention followed by legislative stalemate in Washington, even as individual states such as Oregon have tightened their own rules.
What is not in question is what Thursday looked like from the inside. A driver on a residential street found himself under fire from a teenager carrying a long gun in the middle of a school day. Within a minute that teenager was shooting through the glass of an elementary school's front doors. Teachers moved more than 400 children into lockdown. Someone outside, armed, decided to go in after him rather than wait. Three minutes after the first 911 call, officers were on scene and the shooter was already dead. And three children who should have gone home at the final bell, along with the teacher responsible for them, did not.
Police said more information, including the identities of the victims and possibly the suspect, would be released Friday as the investigation allows. Krantz, who has now led his department through two mass shootings in four years, offered no timeline. "Unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis, and we must," he said.

sources.news_title: Civilian chases teen gunman, ends deadly Oregon school-shooter attack after four killed - The Daily Bo Snerdley
sources.text:
THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do).
- A civilian followed a 16-year-old gunman into an Oregon elementary school and fatally shot him, police say.
- The attacker killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher. Another child and teacher were critically wounded.
- Police say the teenager shot through locked school doors to get inside. Oregon’s governor praised the civilian for stopping further bloodshed.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time).
A teenage gunman shot his way into an Oregon elementary school Thursday. But someone outside saw what was happening, followed him into the building and confronted him with a gun.
Police say that civilian fatally shot the attacker.
By then, four innocent people were dead — three little children and a teacher. Two others were fighting for their lives.
And while investigators work to establish exactly what happened inside Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, one fact stands out: The person who stopped the gunman wasn’t a responding police officer.
It was a member of the community.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz described the extraordinary sequence during a Thursday evening news conference. “An officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, publicly thanked the civilian. “And to the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life, your actions carry a heavy emotional burden – and my thoughts are with you,” she said.
That’s an extraordinary act of courage. Someone saw an armed attacker entering a school full of children and, rather than fleeing, followed him inside.
Police have not identified that person or explained the circumstances under which the civilian was armed. Those details matter, and investigators are expected to provide more information.
But the broad outline of the attack is already horrifying.
At approximately 12:59 p.m. Pacific time Thursday, October 15, police received a 911 call from a person in a vehicle reporting that someone with a long gun had fired at them. More calls quickly followed from Silver Rail Elementary.
According to Krantz, the 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by shooting through locked doors. The school was directed to lock down at 1:01 p.m. Officers arrived approximately one minute later. The suspect was found dead inside the building after the civilian confrontation.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed. A 7-year-old child and another teacher, 54, were hospitalized in critical condition. BEND, Ore. (AP) — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
Authorities said John had been a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary and had attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
Shooter killed minutes after first 911 call
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck early Thursday afternoon who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Krantz said. The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured, but drove off and called for help.
A second driver, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw John shooting at the truck and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside. He saw John wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times, Krantz said.
Police found John dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Krantz said. John shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Three children ages 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25, were killed, police said. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, Krantz said.
The youngest victim was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The pump-action shotgun the attacker used was bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Man who stopped the shooter a father of 2 at the school
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
Silver Rail Elementary has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming Giamanco — said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
___
Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer, Eric Tucker and Ben Finley in Washington; Jamie Stengle in Dallas; Gene Johnson in Seattle; Ed White in Detroit; Philip Marcelo in New York; and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

sources.news_title: Shooter kills teacher, three children at US elementary school
sources.text:
A teenager shot and killed three children and a teacher on Thursday at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon, police said, adding the assailant was later killed by an armed bystander who pursued him into the building.
Officers rushed to Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, a city of about 100,000 in the nation’s northwest, after reports of a shooter on campus on Thursday afternoon.
The three children who died on the scene were aged five, eight and 11, said Bend police chief Mike Krantz. Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting.
The United States, where firearms are readily available, has a long and painful history of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.
People gathered in the city’s Drake Park on Thursday evening for a candelight vigil remembering the victims.
“I’m in total complete shock, and scared and sad,” said Betsy, who did not give her last name. She spent around 10 minutes contemplating a circle of candles and flowers.
“It’s awful, but it also has brought people together,” she told AFP.
Krantz, the police chief, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun.
Dozens of emergency calls then reported that a shooter had entered the school and all law enforcement in the area were called to the scene, the chief added.
Officers arrived at 1:02 pm local time (2002 GMT) within minutes of the calls, he said.
“Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said.
“Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead.”
One seven-year-old and one 54-year-old teacher with critical injuries were transported to a local hospital, he said.
The police chief said the investigation was in its early stages, but told the press conference it appeared “the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors.”
He added that the 16-year-old shooter was a Bend resident.
– ‘Unthinkable tragedy’ –
Between 400 and 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary, where more than 40 staff work, according to a police spokesperson.
After a lockdown, Bend-La Pine School District said law enforcement was escorting students in buses to a separate location, where families could reunite with their children.
The district’s superintendent, Steve Cook, tearfully called the day’s events “an unthinkable tragedy.”
“We are heartbroken. We are horrified. This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here,” he told reporters.
Parents were anxiously waiting at the site near a church, where Drew Sharp, the father of a fifth grader, the highest grade in the school, told CBS News: “I have faith that he’s okay and that he’ll be alright.”
Children were disembarking from the bus youngest to oldest “which makes sense,” Sharp said, but “it’s just more time waiting.”
Friday classes at schools across the district along with activities and athletic events were canceled, Bend-La Pine said in a statement.
The elementary school is approximately 170 miles (270 kilometers) southeast of the city Portland. It serves primary-age students in kindergarten through fifth grade.
– ‘Cannot keep accepting this’ –
The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.
There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot.
“Our hearts are with the terrified children and the families anxiously waiting to hear that their loved ones are safe,” GIFFORDS, a gun safety organization, said on X.
“We cannot keep accepting this as a fact of life.”
Thursday’s shooting was followed by a painfully familiar chorus of calls for action on gun control, pleas that have resulted in little meaningful change.
In the face of decades of massacres, the powerful US pro-gun lobby has given millions of dollars to primarily conservative politicians in a successful bid to keep gun laws loose.
“They’re killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear,” said Janelle Bynum, an Oregon congresswoman, in a statement.
“This continues to happen,” she said later, speaking on CNN. “And it seems as if the adults don’t care.”
AFP
